summary.text: A brine pool is a body of very salty water collected in a dip in the seafloor, sometimes called an underwater lake.
Its salinity is typically three to eight times that of the surrounding ocean, and the dense brine does not easily mix with the seawater above.
Lacking oxygen, brine pools are deadly to most animals, yet life such as bivalves can be found in a thin band along their rims.

items.prompt: When seawater freezes into sea ice, what happens to the salt it contained?

options.label: It is expelled and sinks as dense brine
It stays locked inside the ice crystals
It turns into a gas and escapes
It forms a crust on top of the ice

items.explain: Salts do not fit into the crystal structure of ice, so they are pushed out and form a cold, dense brine that sinks to the sea floor.

items.prompt: A submersible finds a crab that died in a brine pool years ago, still intact. Why hasn't it rotted?

options.label: The cold water froze it solid
The pool has no oxygen for decay
The deep pressure crushes all bacteria
Scavengers dislike the smell of crab

items.explain: Dead organisms are preserved in the brine for years without decay because the pool is anoxic.

items.prompt: Why can a brine pool look like a lake with its own shoreline on the sea floor?

options.label: A sheet of ice floats over it
It is fresh water trapped in rock
Its dense brine doesn't mix with the water above
A layer of oil seals it off

items.explain: The dense brine does not easily mix with the overlying seawater, so a distinct interface forms between the two water masses.

items.prompt: Brine pools in the Gulf of Mexico get their salt from what source?

options.label: Salt pushed out of sea ice above them
Salt carried in by large rivers
Salt fallen from volcanic ash clouds
Old salt beds from a sea that dried out

items.explain: In the Middle Jurassic the Gulf was a shallow sea that dried out, leaving thick salt that in places now sits at or near the seafloor and dissolves into brine.

items.prompt: Brine pools often hold lots of methane and hydrogen sulfide. What kind of life draws energy from these?

options.label: Chemosynthetic organisms near the pool
Plants photosynthesizing in the dark
Fish that breathe the brine itself
Seabirds diving down to feed there

items.explain: The hydrogen sulfide and methane in the brine provide energy to chemosynthetic organisms living near the pool.

items.prompt: How large can brine pools be?

options.label: Never more than a few metres across
From under 1 m² to about 120 km²
Always larger than a whole city
Never bigger than a small car

items.explain: They range from less than 1 square metre to the 120-square-kilometre Orca Basin.

paragraphs.heading: Lakes on the seafloor
paragraphs.text: A brine pool, also called an underwater lake or brine lake, is a body of brine gathered in a hollow of the seafloor. The brine is dense, with a salinity usually three to eight times higher than the ocean around it. It does not mix easily with the seawater above, so a sharp boundary forms between the two, which is why these pools are called lakes on the sea floor. They range from less than 1 square metre to the 120-square-kilometre Orca Basin.

paragraphs.heading: Three ways to make one
paragraphs.text: Brine pools form in three main ways. In brine rejection, freezing seawater pushes out its salts because they do not fit into ice crystals, and the cold, dense brine sinks to the seafloor and can collect in dips. In salt tectonics, as in the Gulf of Mexico, a shallow sea dried out in the Middle Jurassic and left salt up to 8 km thick; where that salt now reaches the seafloor, seawater dissolves it into brine. In geothermal heating, seawater seeps into cracks at spreading centres, dissolves minerals, is heated over magma, then rises and settles in hollows as brine.

paragraphs.heading: A deadly place to swim
paragraphs.text: Because the brine is dense and deep currents do not stir it, these pools often become anoxic, meaning without oxygen. Without mixing, brine can lose its oxygen within weeks. An animal that swims in tries to breathe, suffers a lack of oxygen to the brain and toxic shock from the extreme salt, and dies quickly unless it can get back to the rim. Submarines and remotely operated vehicles find pools littered with dead fish, crabs and amphipods, which stay preserved for years without decaying.

paragraphs.heading: Life on the shore
paragraphs.text: The brine often holds high levels of hydrogen sulfide and methane, which give energy to chemosynthetic organisms, living things that run on chemical energy, near the pool. Bacteria and their partners grow on the pool's shores where nutrients are released most. Patchy reddish layers of salt-loving archaea can float above the brine's boundary. The shores change sharply in salinity, oxygen, pH and temperature over a short vertical distance, which creates many different niches. Bivalves live in a thin band along the rim, and a new genus and species, Apachecorbula muriatica, was found at the edge of the Valdivia Deep pool in the Red Sea.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are found
paragraphs.text: Brine pools are common below polar sea ice and in the deep ocean. Depending on how concentrated the brine is, minerals such as baryte can come out of it and form crystal crusts around the pool's edge. On an ocean-wide scale, brine rejection is linked to the formation of North Atlantic Deep Water and Antarctic Bottom Water, which play a large part in global thermohaline circulation.
